title: Ocean Animals So Weird They Look Fake. One Has a See-Through Head
description: Animal Secrets #21. This month a fish with a see-through head was filmed in 4K, only the 11th time MBARI has met it in about 7,000 dives. We count down five ocean animals from this month's news that look fake but are real: a whale with a crooked face, a sea pig with a stranger living in its skin, a rock with 245 animals inside, a squid with elbows, and the barreleye. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: This fish has a see-through head. And its eyes move around inside it.

scenes.label: Seen 11 times
scenes.say: Scientists just filmed it in 4K. In nearly forty years of diving, they've met it only eleven times.

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: Okay, so it's number one today. Because at the very end, I'll show you that its two 'eyes' aren't eyes at all.
But first, four more ocean animals from this month's news that honestly look fake. Every one of them is real.

scenes.label: 27.3% mapped
scenes.say: Here's the thing. As of last year, only about 27 percent of the ocean floor had even been mapped properly.

scenes.label: The crooked whale
scenes.say: Number five. A whale with the most crooked face in mammal history.
Its fossil skull came out of the desert in southern Peru, back in the mid-1990s. It was only named this month.

scenes.label: 6 million years
scenes.say: It lived between about 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago. A small cousin of sperm whales, roughly 2.7 meters long.

scenes.label: 'It's damaged'
scenes.say: And when researchers first looked at it, they thought the skull had been squashed after death. It looked broken.

scenes.label: Nostrils: left
scenes.say: It wasn't broken. Both of its bony nostrils sat completely on the left side of its face. Both of them. That's not a deformity. That's design.

scenes.label: Snout 31° down
scenes.say: Its snout curved down by 31 degrees. And its neck let it tip its head down another 55 degrees.
Why build a face like that? Because this whale hunted along the seafloor, in shallow coastal water.

scenes.label: Heavy bone nose
scenes.say: Its nose was packed with dense bone, like built-in diving weights, pulling its head toward the mud.

scenes.label: Sound, not whiskers
scenes.say: It had no whiskers to feel for food. So scientists think it found hidden prey in the mud by sound, with echolocation.

scenes.label: 'Huachafo'
scenes.say: And its name says it all. Huachafo is Peruvian Spanish for flashy, over-the-top, even tacky. Perfect for this face.

scenes.label: The sea pig
scenes.say: Number four. A pig that lives at the bottom of the ocean. Well, sort of.

scenes.label: About 15 cm
scenes.say: It's called a sea pig. It's about fifteen centimeters long, chubby, see-through, and it walks on tube feet like little legs.

scenes.label: A sea cucumber
scenes.say: But it's not a pig. It's actually a sea cucumber, crawling across the deep seafloor and eating rotting stuff in the mud.

scenes.label: Whale-fall party
scenes.say: Sometimes sea pigs crowd together around a dead whale on the seafloor, feasting on the rich mud around it.
Now here's the twist. This month, scientists in Tokyo revealed something living inside its skin.

scenes.label: A hidden guest
scenes.say: A brand new kind of bacteria, hiding in the sea pig's body wall. Nobody had ever seen it before.

scenes.label: Name: Abyssoplasma
scenes.say: Its name starts with 'Abysso', as in the abyss. A tiny life-form living full-time inside a walking sea cucumber.

scenes.label: 649,000 letters
scenes.say: Its DNA is tiny, just 649,000 letters long. It has thrown away almost everything it doesn't need.

scenes.label: Giant proteins
scenes.say: But more than a quarter of that DNA builds giant proteins on its outside. Some are over 5,000 building blocks long.

scenes.label: What's in it for the pig?
scenes.say: So the bacteria clearly need the sea pig. But what does the sea pig get back? Scientists honestly don't know yet.

scenes.label: The living rock
scenes.say: Number three isn't even an animal. It's a rock. And 245 animals were living inside one of them.

scenes.label: Fist-sized
scenes.say: These are deep-sea nodules. Black, lumpy, about the size of your fist, made mostly of iron and manganese.

scenes.label: 4–6 km deep
scenes.say: They lie on the Pacific floor, four to six kilometers down. And they grow only a few millimeters every million years.
Think about that. One of these rocks can sit on the seafloor for millions of years, slowly growing.

scenes.label: 244 rocks
scenes.say: This month, a team cracked open 244 of these nodules. Inside the tiny cracks, they found 4,139 animals.

scenes.label: Under 1 mm
scenes.say: Most of them were smaller than a millimeter. Tiny roundworms, and little crustaceans called copepods.

scenes.label: Avg 17 per rock
scenes.say: On average, each rock held seventeen animals. But one crowded nodule was home to 245.

scenes.label: 1,000 km apart
scenes.say: And here's the weird part. Rock communities a thousand kilometers apart looked alike, but different from the mud right next to them.

scenes.label: Mining target
scenes.say: The problem? These rocks are full of valuable metals. Companies want to mine them. And they take millions of years to grow back.

scenes.label: Gone with the rock?
scenes.say: So if a rock disappears, does its little world disappear too? Scientists say that's exactly what they need to find out next.

scenes.label: The squid with elbows
scenes.say: Number two. A squid with elbows. And arms so long it looks like a ghost dangling spaghetti.

scenes.label: Up to 6.4 m
scenes.say: It's the bigfin squid. The longest one ever measured stretched 6.4 meters, about as long as a small bus.

scenes.label: 90° bend
scenes.say: But that's mostly arms. They stick out sideways, then bend down at ninety degrees, like elbows.

scenes.label: 20× its body
scenes.say: The thin sticky threads hanging down can be up to twenty times longer than its body. Scientists think they work like a fishing net.

scenes.label: About 70 ever
scenes.say: And it's ridiculously rare. Only about seventy bigfin squid have ever been seen or collected. Ever.
The first one was caught in 1883. But science didn't even describe it properly until 1998.

scenes.label: No adult caught
scenes.say: And here's the crazy part. Nobody has ever caught a grown-up bigfin squid. We only know the adults from video.

scenes.label: 6,212 m deep
scenes.say: It also holds a record. One was filmed 6,212 meters down in the Philippine Trench, the deepest squid ever seen.

scenes.label: August 2026
scenes.say: This August, the same institute that filmed today's number one bumped into a bigfin squid off California, over three kilometers down.
It was the first one ever confirmed alive in the Northeast Pacific. So, are you ready for number one?

scenes.label: The barreleye
scenes.say: Number one. The barreleye fish. The fish with a see-through head.

scenes.label: 600 m down
scenes.say: In October, a robot sub was diving about ninety kilometers off California. The fish was hanging about six hundred meters down.

scenes.label: 'STOP!'
scenes.say: The robot was already heading back up. Then researcher Shannon Johnson saw the fish on screen and yelled for the pilots to stop.

scenes.label: 20 minutes
scenes.say: Scientists ran back to the control room. For twenty minutes, they filmed it in 4K. The video got over a hundred thousand views in five days.

scenes.label: Twilight zone
scenes.say: It lives in the twilight zone. Below about two hundred meters, sunlight is so faint that plants can't grow.

scenes.label: Clear dome
scenes.say: Now look at its head. The top is a clear dome, filled with fluid. Like a fishbowl built into its face.

scenes.label: Green tube eyes
scenes.say: Inside sit two big green tubes. Those are its eyes. They point straight up, scanning for shadows passing overhead.

scenes.label: Waiting, not chasing
scenes.say: It barely swims. It just hangs there on its big fins, perfectly still, staring up into the dark.

scenes.label: Shadows above
scenes.say: Down here, lots of animals glow to hide their shadows. So eyes that catch the faintest flicker from above are a huge advantage.

scenes.label: Eyes rotate
scenes.say: But when it spots food, its eyes rotate forward inside the dome. So it can keep its prey in sight as it turns.

scenes.label: Stealing lunch?
scenes.say: And here's a wild idea. Scientists think it may steal small animals caught in the stinging tentacles of jelly-like siphonophores.
If that's true, the clear dome could be a shield, protecting its eyes from the stings. But that's still a hypothesis.

scenes.label: 1939 mistake
scenes.say: For decades, science got this fish wrong. It was named in 1939, from fish pulled up in nets.

scenes.label: Dome destroyed
scenes.say: The nets crushed the fragile dome on the way up. So old drawings showed a normal head, with eyes stuck pointing up.

scenes.label: Solved in 2008
scenes.say: Then in 2008, a netted barreleye survived for a few hours in a ship's tank. Researchers watched its eyes rotate. Mystery solved.

scenes.label: First film: 710 m
scenes.say: And this summer, its cousin, the binocular fish, was filmed alive for the very first time, 710 meters deep in the Atlantic.

scenes.label: The fake 'eyes'
scenes.say: Okay, now the promise from the start. See those two dark spots above its mouth? They look exactly like eyes, right?

scenes.label: They're nostrils
scenes.say: They're not eyes. They're its nostrils, smelling organs. The real eyes are the green glowing tubes inside its head.

scenes.label: Big fins, small mouth
scenes.say: Even its name is funny. Macropinna microstoma means big fins, small mouth. Not a word about the see-through head.

scenes.label: Countdown recap
scenes.say: A crooked whale, a pig with a stranger in its skin, a living rock, an elbow squid, and a fish with nostrils for a face.

scenes.label: Your pick?
scenes.say: Which one looks the most fake to you? Tell me in the comments, and I'll draw the winner next.

short.title: Its Eyes Are Inside Its Head. Seen 11 Times in 40 Years
short.header: The fish with a see-through head
short.description: MBARI filmed the barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma) in 4K about 600 m deep off California: only its 11th encounter in about 7,000 dives. Its eyes rotate inside a clear dome, and the 'eyes' on its face are nostrils. Full countdown of 5 fake-looking ocean animals on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: You can see this fish's eyes right through its head. And almost nobody has seen it alive.

scenes.label: 11 in 7,000 dives
scenes.say: Scientists have done about seven thousand robot dives here. They've met this fish only eleven times. They just filmed it in 4K.

scenes.label: Clear dome
scenes.say: Its head is a clear dome full of fluid. The green tubes inside are its eyes, staring straight up.

scenes.label: 600 m down
scenes.say: It hangs six hundred meters down, perfectly still, staring up. When food passes, its eyes rotate forward inside the dome.

scenes.label: Nets crushed it
scenes.say: For decades, nets crushed that fragile dome on the way up, so science drew it with a normal head. Totally wrong.

scenes.label: Those are nostrils
scenes.say: And those two dark spots on its face? Nostrils. Because this fish's eyes are inside its head.
